I remember seeing a mangosteen martini on the drinks menu of a swank Soho bistro  -- maybe man about town Steve M. can speak to an evening with a mangosteen, but I dare say I've never met one. 

However, a NYT food critic wrote this in 2003:

"I'm a big-time mangosteen addict, which presents problems.

The mangosteen -- a tropical fruit about the size of a tangerine, whose leathery maroon shell surrounds moist, fragrant, snow-white segments of ambrosial flesh -- can't get a visa. Mangosteens may not legally be imported into the United States. They may not legally be shipped to the mainland from Hawaii, where a few sturdy souls have lately begun to grow them anyway.

Here in Thailand and elsewhere in Southeast Asia, notably Vietnam and Singapore, people buy them by the bagful for small change. In Vancouver and other Canadian cities with big Asian populations, you can find them at street markets and greengrocers. In Paris, Fauchon will sell you one for a prince's if not quite a king's ransom.

But back home in Washington, the best I can do without jumping on a plane is the wooden mangosteen, handsomely carved and oiled, that sits on my desk there.

***

Apparently things have changed, slightly, and for the better. Imagine that, something has improved since 2003! And that is, you can now buy mangosteens in the US. The catch is they start at $119 for 3lb boxes. Maybe they'll go on sale.

I have mixed feelings about this one.  Some lively long answers; some terrific cluing (BINGE WATCHING; CLOWN NOSE; BARCAR (the hardest for me to see).  But all those pop singers!  ADELE was easy once I eliminated Swift; Taylor was too long.  Does ADELE have "Ages" while Taylor has "Eras"?  These self-proclaiming singers have some nerve to name entire time periods after themselves.  Would Barbara Cook have done that?  Ella Fitzgerald?  Frank Sinatra, even?  Barbra Streisand certainly has a healthy ego, but she never did that.

I got ADELE with no help.  IGOR came in.  But I had to cheat on LEANN to finish the puzzle.  Sorry, honey, but if you think I'm GONNA sit here till the cows come home on a gorgeous day in NYC, you've got another think coming.

One question:  Are the MANGO and the MANGOSTEEN the same fruit or different fruits?  Once I had written in MANGO(S) I sort of felt I was finished.

So I had to WAKE up at 4:30 a.m., not because LIFE'S TOO SHORT and I have an urge to  glimpse the MORNING STAR to feel I LIVE, but for a SCAN appointment at 5:45 in one of those UFO/ET TUbes they put you in when you've HIT A SNAG in the wellness department (and  telling mom about it is part of the fun because she'll lovingly always say , "Oh honey, I'm sorry I can't help you; the factory is closed and the warranty is expired" lol.)

Funny how time flies when you're BINGE WATCHING a great show, but gets to being OVERLONG when you're lying motionless in an MRI machine. 

When the SCAN was done, I turned to the radiologist,  letting him know I was fine when asked how I was doing, and adding, perplexed,  "But HERE'S THE THING BEFORE I GO, this baby must cost at least a cool MIL and still they can't get it to be cushy and comfortable?"

"I KNOW, right?" he replied. "And you got the newest model. You should see the older one in the other room!"

So I started the day counting my WINs. After all, I got CATERED to with the (brand new) Ferrari of MRI machines!  
I drove home, still bleary-eyed, BUT with a smile on my face, and feeling lucky.

Unlike the other planets, we are never between Venus (or Mercury) and the Sun.  That's impossible because our orbit is outside theirs.

So, unlike Mars and the rest, we never see Venus or Mercury more than a certain number of angular degrees from the Sun.  For Venus that's about 45 degrees or about 1/2 way from "straight up" to the horizon.  For Mercury it ranges between 18 and 28 degrees.  These extremes are called "greatest eastern" and "greatest western" elongations.  

When the sun sets before the planet sets, it's an "evening star".  And when the planet rises before the sun rises, it's called a "morning star".

Much of the time these planets are too near the sun to be seen--they are lost in the glare.  And most of the time when they are directly in front of the sun or directly behind the sun, they are a little off line, a little too high or too low, to actually "eclipse" the Sun, or to be eclipsed by the Sun.  In either case we'd struggle to see them at this point.

Except...very occasionally one of them actually passes in front of the Sun.  That is called a transit, and the planet shows up as a tiny dark disc against the solar brilliance.

The last transit of Mercury was in 2012, and the next one will be in 2032.  The last transit of Venus was 2018, and the next one will be in 2117.

In about 69,000 years, there will be a simultaneous transit of both planets.  

I can hardly wait.
